reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents and criticizes a OneCoin promotional presentation rather than endorsing participation in it. The quoted speaker promotes paid education packages and token mining, while the video frames the claims skeptically, including the visible criticism that the 5000€ education is worth no more than 10€ and the closing label "THE BLACKLIST."

citations.quote: we're not selling currency, we're not selling tokens, we're actually selling something called online education

opening.argument: The offer links a substantial payment to a digital-asset benefit and an immediate participation instruction. The speaker says buyers pay for a Tycoon package, receive free tokens, can mine OneCoin, and should “come in, mine your coins.” That is not merely a discussion of education: it presents the viewer’s payment and enrollment as the route to obtaining and using the tokens. The profit framing reinforces the inducement, since “the more you know” is directly tied to profiting. Calling the purchase an education package does not remove the promised asset acquisition attached to the action.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the phrase “online education” as if it exhausted the offer. It does not explain away the separate promise of free tokens, the instruction to mine OneCoin, or the stated €5,000 payment. Nor does a critical caption prove that the underlying solicitation is absent; it can instead identify what is being promoted and then criticize its value. The relevant question is what action-benefit relationship the presentation contains, and that relationship is explicit.

citations.quote: we're not selling currency, we're not selling tokens, we're actually selling something called online education
And of course, in our Education Packages we get free tokens

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These quotations show only what a speaker in the presentation says, not that the video endorses it. The surrounding framing identifies the material as something being examined: the supplied title calls it “EDUCATION PLANS,” while the closing visual says “THE BLACKLIST,” and another visual explicitly says the education is worth no more than 10€. The quoted promise is therefore evidence under criticism, not evidence that viewers are being solicited by this video.

opening.argument: Several concrete warning signals appear together: a €5,000 top-tier package, a requirement to upgrade to obtain level 5, tokens supplied through the package, mining language, profit language, and a limited-time push. The speaker does not present these as unrelated facts; the package is the gateway to the token and mining opportunity, while success is tied to knowing more and upgrading. That combination makes the education label look like a wrapper around paid mining participation. The urgency statement, “This opportunity only is now,” adds pressure to act before the viewer can independently assess what the package or tokens are worth.

citations.quote: The more you know the more you will profit
The level 5 is in the Tycoon package. So everybody needs to at least upgrade to the top package to get level 5.
you pay 5000 euros for a Tycoon package

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense points to skeptical presentation elements, but those elements do not negate the underlying red flags. Calling the material a critique cannot make the €5,000 price, compulsory top-package upgrade, profit claim, or limited-time language disappear. The criticism may establish that the editor objects to the offer; it does not establish that the offer lacks the solicitation pattern shown in the quoted presentation.

citations.quote: So everybody needs to at least upgrade to the top package to get level 5.
This opportunity only is now.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The red flags are precisely why the video presents the material critically. The evidence does not show this video asking viewers to buy, register, or contact anyone; it shows a quoted presentation being displayed alongside explicit negative evaluation. “This education for 5000€ is worth no more than 10€” contradicts the offer’s value claim rather than amplifying it, and “THE BLACKLIST” signals condemnation rather than a sales prompt.

opening.argument: The apparent educational framing functions as a participation pitch because the proposed learning is repeatedly tied to financial success and access to tokens. The program is described as the product being sold, the audience is told to upgrade to the Tycoon package, and the closing instruction is to come in and mine coins. A presentation can call itself education while still steering viewers toward a paid asset-acquisition pathway. The presence of a formal event setting and a named academy further supports that this is organized promotion, not neutral background information.

citations.quote: This is our product, we are selling EDUCATION PACKAGES.
So everybody needs to at least upgrade to the top package to get level 5.
This opportunity only is now. It means come in, mine your coins, and that's it.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense assumes that critical editing changes the role of the material being shown. But the speaker’s own words still present the academy as the product, connect it to profit and tokens, and direct participation. A warning can reproduce a promotional pitch while still showing the pitch; the fact that the editor later condemns it does not change the solicitation structure visible in the source material.

citations.quote: This is our product, we are selling EDUCATION PACKAGES.
The more you know the more you will profit
It means come in, mine your coins, and that's it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument confuses the role of the embedded speaker with the role of the video. The supplied title identifies the subject as “EDUCATION PLANS,” and the video ends with “THE BLACKLIST,” while its visual criticism says the €5,000 education is worth no more than €10. Those signals frame the sales pitch as an object of scrutiny. The speaker’s directive therefore does not establish that this video steers viewers toward participation.
